<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Anita Kriz
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_contribution ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Authors contributed equally.</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Antonin Berthon<span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotemark"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotemark: </span>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
        </span></span></span>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Nicolás Astorga
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mihaela van der Schaar
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

</span>

</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{ak2680,armb3}@cam.ac.uk</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite their extensive pretraining knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) struggle to adaptively gather information in experimental design tasks. We study how to <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">amortize sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) into an LLM</em> by explicitly training the reasoning that guides action selection using information-gain rewards.
Our approach specifies the experimental generative model independently of the LLM’s own beliefs,
allowing us to optimize expected information gain under a model of our choosing. We investigate the design choices for amortization, including alternative generative-model constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and computational costs relative to training- and inference-time BED baselines.
On Twenty Questions, the resulting policies improve information acquisition and task performance, outperform inference- and training-time BED baselines at substantially lower computational cost,
and generalize to unseen categories. We further demonstrate positive transfer from Twenty Questions training to Medi-Q, a real-world clinical dialogue benchmark.
These results suggest that information gathering can be learned as a generalizable reasoning skill in LLMs.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Many real-world problems are not fully specified upfront, yet humans are remarkably effective at gathering the information needed to solve them <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Consider a clinician diagnosing a patient.
They draw on their medical knowledge to ask about relevant symptoms, think about possible diagnoses, and identify tests that can distinguish between them. As new evidence is acquired, they refine their hypotheses to decide what to investigate next. Effective information gathering thus requires both the prior knowledge to inform decision-making and the ability to continuously adapt those decisions in light of new evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given their extensive pretraining knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored as agents in adaptive decision-making  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashokkumar et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Despite this potential, LLMs have been shown to perform poorly in multi-turn settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krishnamurthy et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laban et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. In particular, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gupta et al. (2025)</a></cite> demonstrate that LLMs are insensitive to experimental feedback, suggesting that their performance relies more on their (potentially inaccurate) prior knowledge than on their ability to adapt their reasoning to new evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">we investigate how to improve LLMs’ ability to adaptively gather information</span>.
Rather than using an LLM to sample informative actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kobalczyk et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hartmann et al., 2026</a>)</cite>,
we hypothesize that learning generalizable information gathering strategies requires explicitly training
the reasoning process that guides action selection.
We formalize this problem through sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rainforth et al. (2023)</a></cite>,
which uses a generative model of the experiment to select actions that reduce uncertainty about an unknown quantity of interest. We investigate how to amortize this information-theoretic objective into an LLM reasoning policy using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Crucially, training-time amortization allows us to specify the experimental generative model <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">independently</span> of the LLM’s own beliefs. This means that we can evaluate actions based on their expected information gain under a model of our choosing.
We additionally investigate whether optimizing information gain over multiple interactions encourages non-myopic information-gathering strategies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We empirically show that amortizing BED into a reasoning LLM develops strategies that generalize to previously unseen domains and tasks. Specifically, we train reasoning LLMs on Twenty Questions and demonstrate improved information acquisition across both seen and unseen categories. We show that models trained in this environment exhibit positive transfer to the real-world clinical dialogue benchmark Medi-Q <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Our results show that decoupling the experimental generative model from the LLM’s beliefs improves information acquisition.
We further find that rewarding expected information-gain rewards under our specified generative model improves learning relative to realized rewards, and that optimizing information acquisition over future interactions can improve sequential information gathering in non-myopic environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contributions.</span> Our contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacktriangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>▶</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\blacktriangleright</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formulate amortized sequential BED for reasoning LLMs and study how to construct its generative model and information-gain reward (Sec. <a href="#S4" title="4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacktriangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>▶</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\blacktriangleright</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate that information-gathering behavior can be amortized into a reasoning LLM, improving information acquisition and transferring across unseen domains and to a different information-gathering task (Sec. <a href="#S5" title="5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacktriangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>▶</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\blacktriangleright</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We systematically study the design of amortized BED, including alternative generative-model constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and their computational cost relative to training- and inference-time BED baselines (Sec. <a href="#S5" title="5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background &amp; Problem Setup</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Bayesian Experimental Design</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> denote an unknown variable that we wish to learn about. To gain information about <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, we can select an experimental design <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, which results in an observation <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, in a diagnostic setting, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> may represent a patient’s underlying condition that we want to identify, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> a diagnostic test, and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> the resulting test outcome. Because experiments may be subject to constraints such as cost or time, the chosen design <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> should be as informative as possible.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">BED provides a framework for quantifying how informative a potential design <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is using a generative model of the experiment, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta,y\mid x)=p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta,y\mid x)=p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math>. Here, the prior <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> represents our initial beliefs about <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> and the likelihood <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math> describes the probability of observing <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> given <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. After selecting <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and observing <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, these beliefs are updated through the posterior <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta\mid y,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta\mid y,x)</annotation></semantics></math>. The informativeness of a potential design <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is then quantified by its expected information gain (EIG):</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{EIG}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>EIG</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathrm{EIG}(x)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,x)}\left[\log p(\theta\mid y,x)-\log p(\theta)\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,x)}\left[\log p(\theta\mid y,x)-\log p(\theta)\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S2.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,x)}\left[\log p(y\mid\theta,x)-\log p(y\mid x)\right]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,x)}\left[\log p(y\mid\theta,x)-\log p(y\mid x)\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">which measures how much information design <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> will provide about <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, in expectation over possible <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> and observations <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>. Using Bayes’ rule, the EIG can be seen as either the expected reduction in uncertainty about <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> after observing <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> (Eq. <a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2.1 Bayesian Experimental Design ‣ 2 Background &amp; Problem Setup ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) or the expected reduction in uncertainty about <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> from knowing <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> (Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="In 2.1 Bayesian Experimental Design ‣ 2 Background &amp; Problem Setup ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The optimal one-step design is defined as <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{\star}=\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{EIG}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>EIG</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{\star}=\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{EIG}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the space of designs. This formulation extends naturally to the sequential setting where the design at step <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is chosen based on the history of previous experiments, <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}=(x_{1},y_{1},\ldots,x_{t-1},y_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}=(x_{1},y_{1},\ldots,x_{t-1},y_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math> by maximizing the EIG under the updated belief <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta\mid h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta\mid h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>. The experimental design at step <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> can then be selected as <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}^{\star}=\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{EIG}(x;h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>EIG</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}^{\star}=\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{EIG}(x;h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Challenges of Design Selection.</span>
Selecting designs according to the EIG in adaptive settings presents two major challenges.
First, optimizing the EIG requires a costly estimation of the posterior <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(\theta\mid x_{1:t},y_{1:t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta\mid x_{1:t},y_{1:t})</annotation></semantics></math> at each step, which depends on the observed interaction history and therefore cannot be computed in advance.
Moreover, even given this posterior, calculating the EIG is doubly intractable: it involves an outer expectation over possible latent states and observations, and an inner marginalization over latent states to compute the posterior predictive distribution <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y_{t}\mid x_{t},h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y_{t}\mid x_{t},h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Repeating this estimation and optimization procedure after every observation can be prohibitively expensive for settings that require decisions to be made in real time.
Second, one-step EIG optimization considers only the immediate next design. This can be suboptimal in non-myopic decision states, where acquiring more information in the future requires first selecting a design with limited immediate information gain.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To address the computational cost of optimizing the EIG at inference time, Deep Adaptive Design (DAD,  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al. (2021)</a></cite>) amortizes sequential experimental design into a design policy <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}(x_{t}\mid h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}(x_{t}\mid h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>, which maps the history <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> to the next design <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This shifts the computational cost to training, allowing the learned policy to directly select the next design at inference time without EIG optimization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Under this design-policy perspective, the standard sequential BED procedure described above corresponds to an implicit policy <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{S}</annotation></semantics></math>, which selects each design by updating the posterior and optimizing the one-step EIG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Amortizing this policy directly would therefore require repeatedly simulating this expensive sequential BED procedure to generate training targets. Instead, DAD observes that the total EIG of a sequential experiment is equal to the sum of its conditional EIGs across steps. Summing these conditional information gains
gives the information gained between the initial prior and the posterior after the complete trajectory. Applying Bayes’ rule then expresses this quantity directly in terms of trajectory likelihoods:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta)p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi)}\left[\log p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi)-\log p(h_{T}\mid\pi)\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta)p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi)}\left[\log p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi)-\log p(h_{T}\mid\pi)\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(h_{T}\mid\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta)}\left[p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi)\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(h_{T}\mid\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta)}\left[p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi)\right].</annotation></semantics></math>
DAD introduces the sequential prior contrastive estimation (sPCE) objective, a lower bound on the total EIG:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{EIG}_{T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta,h_{T}}\!\left[\log\frac{p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi)}{p(h_{T}\mid\pi)}\right]\geq\mathrm{sPCE}_{T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{0:L},h_{T}}\!\left[\log\frac{(L+1)\,p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{0},\pi)}{\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{\ell},\pi)}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>EIG</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mi>log</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>sPCE</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>θ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mi>log</mi><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{EIG}_{T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta,h_{T}}\!\left[\log\frac{p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi)}{p(h_{T}\mid\pi)}\right]\geq\mathrm{sPCE}_{T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{0:L},h_{T}}\!\left[\log\frac{(L+1)\,p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{0},\pi)}{\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{\ell},\pi)}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\theta_{0:L}\sim p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{0:L}\sim p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> form a contrastive set used to approximate the marginal trajectory likelihood. The bound becomes tight as <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, making this design choice a trade-off between estimator bias and computational cost. Importantly, these hypotheses are sampled from the prior rather than from a history-dependent posterior, and therefore do not need to be re-estimated at each experimental step.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau et al. (2022)</a></cite> formulate the sequential design problem as an MDP by decomposing the sparse trajectory-level sPCE objective into per-step rewards:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="r_{t}=\log p(y_{t}\mid\theta_{0},x_{t})-\log\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}C_{t,\ell}+\log\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}C_{t-1,\ell}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></munderover><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>log</mi><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></munderover><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}=\log p(y_{t}\mid\theta_{0},x_{t})-\log\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}C_{t,\ell}+\log\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}C_{t-1,\ell},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{t,\ell}=\prod_{k=1}^{t}p(y_{k}\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∏</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{t,\ell}=\prod_{k=1}^{t}p(y_{k}\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{k})</annotation></semantics></math> is the likelihood of the observed outcomes up to step <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> under hypothesis <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, assuming observations are conditionally independent of the previous history given the hypothesis and current design. They then use a learned critic to estimate the expected future sPCE return, enabling non-myopic policy optimization.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<td id="S3.T1.2.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top" style="padding:-0.5pt 1.5pt;">

</span></td>

</span></td>

<span id="S3.T1.2.8.5.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:71.3pt;">

</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.8.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top" style="padding:-0.5pt 1.5pt;">

</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.2.9" class="ltx_tr">

</span></td>
