</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span><span id="S3.T1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Policy structure and information-value estimation across prior methods and AR-BED.</span> Policy notation is schematic: <math id="S3.T1.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is the interaction history and <math id="S3.T1.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> an explicit reasoning trace (Eq. <a href="#S4.E5" title="In 4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>); parameter and time indices are omitted. <sup id="S3.T1.6" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.T1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">†</span></sup>Candidate proposals are followed by inference-time EIG selection. Indented rows denote ablations; shading marks changes and — denotes an unchanged prior or likelihood. Misspecification restricts the coverage of <math id="S3.T1.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> and the training targets, while retaining a fixed prior over <math id="S3.T1.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math>. Section references point to experimental analyses.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BED-based information gathering with LLMs has been studied through inference-time design selection and training-time policy optimization. Inference-time methods estimate EIG using LLM-induced generative models and select among candidate questions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kobalczyk et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al., 2025</a>)</cite>; CA-BED extends this approach to non-myopic selection through conversation-tree planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arnould et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. ASIG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hartmann et al., 2026</a>)</cite> instead amortizes design selection into an LLM policy, while retaining a generative model derived from the policy LLM’s predictive distributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our approach explicitly optimizes the reasoning preceding design selection, constructs the training generative model independently of the policy LLM, and uses expected information rewards over multiple steps to allow for non-myopic information gathering. Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Related Work: BED within Large Language Models ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the modeling and training choices across prior methods and our ablations. We discuss related works in detail in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Extended Related Works ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our goal is to amortize sequential BED into a reasoning LLM. One approach to using an LLM as a policy is to directly sample a design given an interaction history, <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}(x_{t}\mid h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}(x_{t}\mid h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>, and optimize its expected information gain <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hartmann et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Instead, our aim is to train an LLM that can <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">reason through limited information</span>: deliberating over which hypotheses remain plausible, how possible observations distinguish them, and which further experiments those observations may enable.
We therefore parameterize the policy as</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}(z_{t},x_{t}\mid h_{t-1})=\pi_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid h_{t-1})\cdot\pi_{\phi}(x_{t}\mid h_{t-1},z_{t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}(z_{t},x_{t}\mid h_{t-1})=\pi_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid h_{t-1})\cdot\pi_{\phi}(x_{t}\mid h_{t-1},z_{t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">and train its joint output <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(z_{t},x_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(z_{t},x_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> with an information gain objective.
At a high level, our training procedure consists of three steps:</p>
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generate a design through reasoning.</span> Given an interaction history <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, the policy generates a reasoning trace <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> followed by a design <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluate its information value.</span> A generative model, specified independently of the policy, provides the hypothesis and outcome distributions used to compute the information gain of the design <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimize the reasoning policy.</span> We use information-gain rewards accumulated over <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-step rollouts to train the reasoning policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This procedure requires two main design choices: how to construct the generative model used to evaluate information gain (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 How should the generative model 𝑝(𝜃,𝑦,𝑥) be constructed? ‣ 4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>), and how to turn this information signal into a training reward (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 How should the reward be assigned? ‣ 4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>How should the generative model <math id="S4.SS1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta,y;x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta,y;x)</annotation></semantics></math> be constructed?</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Estimating the EIG requires specifying a generative model <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta,y;x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta,y;x)</annotation></semantics></math> of the experiment. In our amortized setting, this choice determines both the quality of the training signal and the computational cost of obtaining it. We build on the contrastive formulation in Sec. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design ‣ 2 Background &amp; Problem Setup ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>, which requires specifying two components: a prior <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> over contrastive hypotheses and a likelihood <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math> for evaluating proposed designs. We describe how we construct these components below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decoupling the generative model from the policy.</span>
One option is to use the policy LLM itself to estimate both components, as in the approaches discussed in Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 Related Work: BED within Large Language Models ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Training-time amortization enables an important flexibility: the generative model can instead be specified independently of the policy being trained, without requiring it for design selection at inference time. This allows us to define the experimental distribution used for training upfront, while keeping it fixed as the policy is updated (see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS6" title="D.6 Decoupling the Generative Model from the Policy ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.6</span></a>). This is particularly useful when the initial policy provides a poor approximation of that distribution. For example, the training prior can place mass on hypotheses that the policy itself would be unlikely to generate, while a separate likelihood model can provide more reliable estimates of <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math> than the policy’s own predictive distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The prior <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span>
The contrastive hypotheses can be sampled from the prior for each trajectory, as in sPCE, or fixed across training. We define our prior as a uniform distribution over a finite contrastive set <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta_{C}=\{\theta_{\ell}\}_{\ell=0}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta_{C}=\{\theta_{\ell}\}_{\ell=0}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{C}(\theta_{\ell})=1/(L+1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{C}(\theta_{\ell})=1/(L+1)</annotation></semantics></math>. This prior is fixed across all training trajectories and defines the hypothesis distribution with respect to which information gain is computed. The size of the set introduces a trade-off between coverage and computational cost, while its composition and prior weights determine which hypotheses the policy is trained to distinguish.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The likelihood <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span>
In an open-ended natural-language design space, the possible designs <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> cannot generally be enumerated in advance, making it impractical to precompute their likelihoods. We therefore use a separate, larger LLM as a semantic likelihood evaluator <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math>, which can be queried during training. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau et al. (2022)</a></cite>, we assume that each observation is conditionally independent of the interaction history given the hypothesis and current design, allowing us to accumulate likelihoods as <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{t,\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{t,\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> (see Sec. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design ‣ 2 Background &amp; Problem Setup ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>). The observation <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> may be stochastic even when <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is known. For example, the answer to “Is it cute?” is ambiguous for a fixed <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We therefore retain the full likelihood distribution over the finite outcome space <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Y}</annotation></semantics></math>. Each possible outcome <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> induces a corresponding updated likelihood, <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{t,\ell}^{(y)}=C_{t-1,\ell}p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{t,\ell}^{(y)}=C_{t-1,\ell}p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, which allows us to marginalize over possible outcomes when computing the reward (discussed in Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 How should the reward be assigned? ‣ 4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>). This design also allows for likelihood evaluations <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> to be cached and reused across training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>How should the reward be assigned?</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having specified the generative model in Sec. <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 How should the generative model 𝑝(𝜃,𝑦,𝑥) be constructed? ‣ 4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>, we now consider how information gain over the training hypothesis space should be converted into a reward and how these rewards should be aggregated into training returns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Computing the Reward.</span>
A natural choice is to use the realized incremental sPCE reward in Eq. <a href="#S2.E4" title="In 2.2 Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design ‣ 2 Background &amp; Problem Setup ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, which can be written as</p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}^{\mathrm{real}}=\log\frac{p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y_{t}\mid\theta^{\star},x_{t})}{p_{C}(y_{t}\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>real</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}^{\mathrm{real}}=\log\frac{p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y_{t}\mid\theta^{\star},x_{t})}{p_{C}(y_{t}\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{C}(y\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{C}(y\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the posterior predictive distribution and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})=\frac{C_{t-1,\ell}}{\sum_{j}C_{t-1,j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msub><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mi>j</mi></msub></mstyle><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})=\frac{C_{t-1,\ell}}{\sum_{j}C_{t-1,j}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the posterior over the fixed contrastive hypothesis space under the uniform prior (see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Fixed Contrastive Sets as Finite Bayesian Models ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a> for the full derivation).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For a sampled target <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> and observed outcome <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, this assigns the proposed design its realized information gain. When <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\theta^{\star}\sim p_{C}(\cdot\mid h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{\star}\sim p_{C}(\cdot\mid h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="y_{t}\sim p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(\cdot\mid\theta^{\star},x_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>oracle</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}\sim p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(\cdot\mid\theta^{\star},x_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, the expectation of this reward is exactly the one-step EIG under the current finite belief.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Because our hypothesis and outcome spaces are finite and enumerable, we can bring this expectation inside each training step: rather than relying on a single realized <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\theta^{\star},y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\theta^{\star},y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> pair, we marginalize over both hypotheses and outcomes at each turn. We then assign the expected information reward</p>
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}^{\mathrm{EIG}}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})\left[\log p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})-\log p_{C}(y\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>EIG</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>oracle</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}^{\mathrm{EIG}}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})\left[\log p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})-\log p_{C}(y\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">Under the sampling assumptions above, <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="r_{t}^{\mathrm{EIG}}=\mathbb{E}[r_{t}^{\mathrm{real}}\mid h_{t-1},x_{t}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>EIG</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>real</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}^{\mathrm{EIG}}=\mathbb{E}[r_{t}^{\mathrm{real}}\mid h_{t-1},x_{t}]</annotation></semantics></math>. This is the Rao–Blackwellized form of the realized reward, removing the variance associated with sampling a particular <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\theta^{\star},y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\theta^{\star},y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> pair at a given history and design. The resulting reward is exactly the one-step EIG over the specified finite hypothesis space, though not necessarily over the full hypothesis space of interest (see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS4" title="D.4 Realized versus Expected Information Rewards ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, we may want to use a large contrastive set to provide a rich information-gain signal, but generate training trajectories from only a smaller subset of hypotheses for computational efficiency. In this case, realized and expected rewards can differ beyond variance reduction, as we discuss further in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS5" title="D.5 When the Training-Target Distribution Differs from the Contrastive Prior ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Constructing the Return.</span>
The reward in Eq. <a href="#S4.E7" title="In 4.2 How should the reward be assigned? ‣ 4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> measures only the immediate information value of a design. However, a design may also enable more informative future interactions. Following the sequential formulation of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau et al. (2022)</a></cite>, the undiscounted sum of per-step information rewards recovers multi-step EIG in expectation when rollouts follow the specified generative model. We therefore evaluate each proposed design through a rollout of the current policy. We limit the horizon to <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> steps for tractability and introduce <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> to discount future information:</p>
<table id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{t,K,\gamma}=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\gamma^{k}r_{t+k}^{\mathrm{EIG}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mi>EIG</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{t,K,\gamma}=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\gamma^{k}r_{t+k}^{\mathrm{EIG}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.2" class="ltx_p">Setting <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=1</annotation></semantics></math> recovers the myopic objective, while <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> rewards the initial decision for information acquired at subsequent steps.
In practice, our TQ implementation prunes low-weight hypotheses and advances rollouts using the oracle’s most likely answer rather than sampling an outcome. We discuss these approximations to the fully stochastic objective further in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Non-Myopic Information Returns ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

</div>

</figure>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training Environment</span>
Following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kobalczyk et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hartmann et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, we use Twenty Questions (TQ), where an agent must identify a hidden target within 20 questions. Here, <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is the target (e.g., “horse”), <math id="S5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is an open-ended natural-language question (e.g., “Is it a mammal?”), and the observation lies in the finite answer space <math id="S5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Y}=\{\text{yes},\text{no},\text{maybe}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mtext>yes</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>no</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>maybe</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Y}=\{\text{yes},\text{no},\text{maybe}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. We use <span id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GPT-5</span> as the semantic likelihood evaluator <math id="S5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y|\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y|\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training Data</span>
Our main experiments train on the <span id="S5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Animals</span> domain. We use a fixed contrastive set of 200 animals for computing the training reward, of which 100 are used as ground-truth targets <math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> when constructing training trajectories. We use <span id="S5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GPT-5</span> to generate 250 Twenty Questions games over these 100 targets. From each game, we sample up to five intermediate points before the final guess, yielding 1,200 partial trajectories. Each sampled trajectory defines a history <math id="S5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> containing the sequence of questions and answers observed up to that point. The task-transfer experiment uses a separate training dataset, described in Sec. <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Generalization to other tasks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation Data.</span>
Each model plays 50 Twenty Questions games across three seeds, with a different target sampled for each game in the corresponding evaluation domain. We evaluate on held-out animals drawn from the same 200-animal contrastive set used during training.
In Sec. <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Ablations and Insights ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>, we consider animals that are absent from both the training targets and the training contrastive set. To assess cross-domain transfer, we evaluate on <span id="S5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Plants</span>, <span id="S5.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Celebrities</span>, and <span id="S5.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Countries</span>. Sec. <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Generalization to other tasks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a> evaluates task transfer by applying models trained on Twenty Questions to <span id="S5.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">mediQ</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, an interactive medical question-asking benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models and Hyperparameters</span>
We call our method <em id="S5.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Amortized Reasoning for Bayesian Experimental Design</em> (AR-BED). Unless otherwise specified, <math id="S5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> is a <span id="S5.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Gemma-4-E4B-it</span> reasoning policy trained with expected information rewards with rollout horizon <math id="S5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>. We denote by <math id="S5.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{K}^{\mathrm{Direct}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>BED</mi><mi>K</mi><mi>Direct</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{K}^{\mathrm{Direct}}</annotation></semantics></math> the ablation where we train without reasoning, directly sampling and rewarding a question from the history <math id="S5.p5.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="x\sim p(.|h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\sim p(.|h)</annotation></semantics></math>. We use a batch size of 128 with 8 rollouts per state, and train for 250 steps. For multi-step training (<math id="S5.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>), we set <math id="S5.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=0.5</annotation></semantics></math>. Full training details are in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Additional Experimental Details ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metrics.</span>
We report the solve rate within a 20-question budget and the average EIG per turn to account for varying game lengths.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Amortizing BED into Reasoning Improves General Information Acquisition</h3>

<figure id="S5.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.20832v1/figures/reasoning.png" id="S5.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/122;" width="548" height="122" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S5.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Amortizing BED into reasoning improves information acquisition and transfer.</span>
Bars and bands show mean <math id="S5.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> SEM over three evaluation repeats.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span>
We evaluate whether amortizing BED into the reasoning process improves information acquisition both in- and out-of-distribution. We compare our model, <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, to four controls: the <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Base</span> model and the directly trained <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}^{\mathrm{Direct}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>Direct</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}^{\mathrm{Direct}}</annotation></semantics></math> model, each evaluated with and without reasoning at inference time. This design separates gains from BED training from gains due only to enabling reasoning at test time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span> (Fig. <a href="#S5.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 5.1 Amortizing BED into Reasoning Improves General Information Acquisition ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>)
Adding reasoning to the <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Base</span> model <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">reduces</span> final solve rate across all categories and increases average EIG only on Countries. This suggests that inference-time reasoning alone does not improve information gathering, and may even worsen it.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            A similar effect is observed for some models reported in Table 1 of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</span></span></span> Training a non-reasoning policy improves the in-distribution behavior but the transfer to out-of-distribution domains is inconsistent: it is worse than <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Base</span> on Plants but improves on Celebrities and Countries. This suggests that direct amortization can learn useful in-distribution question-sampling behavior, but does not
produce robust transfer across domains. In contrast, our model <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> achieves the best final solve rate across all categories and obtains the highest average EIG per turn on Animals, Plants, and Countries. These gains over both the <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Base</span> model and the direct policy suggest that training a reasoning model may enable general information-gathering strategies.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Amortizing BED into reasoning outperforms Inference- and Training-Time BED Baselines</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span>
We next compare against BED-style alternatives that differ in how they obtain the generative model used to estimate EIG. Our <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> model uses an external generative model, whereas <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BED-LLM</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al., 2025</a>)</cite> uses the LLM itself to construct the predictive generative model at inference time. We also compare to <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ASIG</span>, a training-time amortization baseline, which uses the same BED-LLM-style LLM-generated model during training but trains a direct question-sampling policy rather than a reasoning policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hartmann et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. To isolate the effect of the information-gain objective, we do not include an additional game reward for <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ASIG</span>. We evaluate <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ASIG</span> with and without reasoning at inference.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:38%;">
<table id="S5.T2.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span><math id="S5.T2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.T2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> is more efficient at both inference and training time.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span>
Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.3 Ablations and Insights ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> outperforms the inference-time and training-time BED baselines on most domains. <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BED-LLM</span> improves only modestly over the reasoning <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Base</span> model, and is worse than the non-reasoning <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Base</span> model on some domains in both solve rate and EIG. This suggests that online BED with an LLM-generated model of the experiment may be limited by the model’s ability to represent the relevant distributions <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math>. Similarly, <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ASIG</span> without reasoning does not improve over the non-reasoning <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Base</span> model, indicating that directly amortizing this LLM-generated BED objective suffers from similar limitations. Adding reasoning at inference substantially improves <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ASIG</span>, but it still remains below <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> on Animals, Plants, and Countries, and is comparable on Celebrities. These results suggest that the benefit comes from amortizing the information-gain objective into the model’s reasoning process and using an external generative model that provides a more reliable training signal.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Amortizing BED into reasoning outperforms Inference- and Training-Time BED Baselines ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows that at inference time, <span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BED-LLM</span> is about <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="61\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>61</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">61\times</annotation></semantics></math> slower per game than <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> because it performs BED computation online. At training time, <span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ASIG</span> is about <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.9\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.9</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.9\times</annotation></semantics></math> slower per step due to the additional cost of using the LLM-generated BED-LLM-style generative model. Thus, <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> gains stronger information acquisition capabilities while avoiding the main computational costs of BED methods with a policy-based generative model.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;"><img src="2610.20832v1/figures/mammals.png" id="S5.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:220/147;" width="220" height="147" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S5.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generalization across held-out animal subgroups.</span>
Solve rate over turns for held-out mammals and non-mammals. Bands show mean <math id="S5.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> SEM over three evaluation repeats.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Ablations and Insights</h3>

<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.20832v1/figures/generative.png" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/123;" width="548" height="123" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S5.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison to BED baselines.</span> <math id="S5.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> outperforms inference-time <span id="S5.F3.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BED-LLM</span> and training-time <span id="S5.F3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ASIG</span> on most domains; bars and bands show mean <math id="S5.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> SEM over evaluation repeats.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.3.1 </span>Misspecified Priors and Size of the Contrastive Set</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To study the effect of a misspecified prior (i.e., training a model with a flawed contrastive set), we compare two variants of <math id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>: one with a 100-animal contrastive set trained on only these animals, and one with a 100-mammal contrastive set trained only on these mammals. Both models are prompted to guess in the category <span id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Animals</span>. As a result, the mammals-trained model received a flawed information signal compared to the true hypothesis space <math id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>: for example, the question “Is it a mammal?” receives <math id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="EIG\approx 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">EIG\approx 0</annotation></semantics></math> despite being a strong question to discriminate between animals.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S5.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 5.2 Amortizing BED into reasoning outperforms Inference- and Training-Time BED Baselines ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the solve rate of both models on held-out sets of 25 mammals and 25 non-mammals. The model trained with a mammals-only contrastive set performs significantly worse than both the animals-trained and base models on non-mammals, suggesting that it learned a flawed representation of the animals hypothesis space. Notably, it also leads to worse performance than the animals-trained model on mammal targets. This suggests that training on the broader hypothesis space of animals might provide exposure to a diversity of features that is beneficial even within the shared mammal subset.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We additionally investigate the effect of the size of the contrastive set in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Contrastive set ablations ‣ Appendix B Extended Experimental Results ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>, finding that using a 200-sample contrastive set improves the OOD transfer performance compared to a 100-sample contrastive set.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.3.2 </span>Using expected or realized IG in the reward signal</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Marginalizing over hypotheses and answers generally provides a stronger training signal than using the realized information gain: expected-reward training improves both EIG and solve rate on Animals, Plants, and Countries, although not on Celebrities. Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Expected versus realized information rewards ‣ Appendix B Extended Experimental Results ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a> reports the matched comparison, consistent with the variance-reduction motivation in Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 How should the reward be assigned? ‣ 4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.3.3 </span>Using a non-myopic reward signal</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Non-myopic information acquisition ‣ Appendix B Extended Experimental Results ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a> brings together three complementary evaluations of multi-step rewards. In a natural-language adaptation of Cube-NM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schütz et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, the two-step policy learns to acquire initially uninformative context for its downstream benefit, substantially outperforming the one-step policy in later disease identification. On the TwentyQuestions target-prediction task of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, multi-step policies improve attribute prediction, particularly on medium and hard questions. Finally, we empirically investigate the extent to which Twenty Questions as played by the GPT-5 policy shows signs of non-myopicity. We show that immediate- and downstream-EIG rankings can differ, while matched-state evaluations find some gains from <math id="S5.SS3.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS3.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=3</annotation></semantics></math> over <math id="S5.SS3.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=1</annotation></semantics></math> at two- and three-question horizons. Together, these results distinguish a controlled non-myopic mechanism from the smaller benefits of lookahead in open-ended questioning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Generalization to other tasks</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The preceding experiments examine transfer across domains within TQ. We now
ask whether the learned information-gathering behavior also transfers
<span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">to a different task</span>. We use MediQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which simulates
clinical questioning: given partial patient information and a multiple-choice
medical inquiry, a policy asks open-ended questions to gather evidence from
an LLM-based Patient with full access to patient records.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span> We construct three synthetic medical TQ environments—
dermatology, neurology, and gastroenterology—each with a 50-disease
contrastive set drawn from MediQ’s answer inventory. Using the
<math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> objective, we train a separate medical policy on
1,200 starting states and evaluate its checkpoint against the
base model. Both policies ask five questions with GPT-5 as the fixed Patient.
We evaluate the quality of each model’s line of questioning by using a
separate GPT-5 decider to predict the answer from the initial information and interaction history.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We report two diagnosis subsets: 95 dermatology cases whose correct diagnoses
are absent from the training contrastive set (<span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">same domain, different
task, held-out labels</span>), and 92 cases from other specialties, including
pediatrics, psychiatry, and cardiology (<span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">different domain and task</span>).
Full training and evaluation details are in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS4" title="C.4 MediQ Experiment ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Details ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
