<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span><span id="S5.T3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance on MediQ after training on Twenty Questions.</span>
Each policy conducts five question–answer turns with a fixed GPT-5 Patient; a separate GPT-5 decider predicts the final answer from the resulting history. Values are means <math id="S5.T3.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 1</annotation></semantics></math> SEM across cases
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span> Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.4 Generalization to other tasks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that medical
<math id="S5.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> improves accuracy from <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="94.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>94.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">94.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> on
held-out dermatology diagnoses and from <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="84.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>84.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">84.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> on other
specialties. It also increases the probability assigned to the correct answer
and reduces the Brier score in both domains. These results indicate that the
reasoning capabilities learned by <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> in a synthetic
TQ environment transfer to a realistic, simulated clinical dialogue setting,
including medical specialties not used during fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We studied how sequential Bayesian experimental design can be amortized into a reasoning LLM to improve adaptive information gathering. Our approach makes two key design choices: decoupling the experimental generative model from the policy to avoid relying on potentially poor predictive distributions, and constructing expected information-gain rewards that can be accumulated across interactions. We find that our method improves information acquisition across unseen hypothesis spaces, outperforming other methods, and that the learned behavior transfers to Medi-Q, a real-world clinical dialogue dataset. Our results suggest that adaptive information gathering can be learned as a transferable reasoning capability in LLMs rather than reconstructed through explicit search at every interaction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations.</span> We study relatively short rollout horizons. Extending the approach to longer horizons while maintaining a reliable training signal is an important direction. We also find that performance is sensitive to the coverage of the contrastive hypothesis set when it is misspecified relative to the true hypothesis space. Further understanding how the size, composition, and prior weighting of the contrastive set affect learning and transfer is therefore an important avenue for future study.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">AI Use Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with the coding implementation, figure editing, LaTeX formatting, and manuscript polishing. The authors determined the research questions, methodology, experiments, and final interpretation of results. We reviewed all AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the final content of this paper.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Extended Related Works</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inference-time BED.</span>
Methods for task disambiguation and adaptive questioning use LLM-generated hypotheses and response predictions to select questions by estimated EIG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kobalczyk et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al., 2025</a>)</cite>; related agents maintain explicit Bayesian beliefs to guide exploration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grand et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
These approaches require repeated belief maintenance and utility evaluation at deployment. While one-step EIG selection is myopic, uncertainty-aware planning and conversation-tree search incorporate simulated future interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arnould et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Thus, non-myopic information gathering is not unique to trained policies; our aim is to amortize this behavior into a reasoning LLM rather than perform explicit design search at inference time.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training-time BED.</span>
Information-driven post-training uses EIG-ranked question preferences <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazzaccara et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or dense rewards based on changes in the model’s confidence in a known target <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Auzina et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. These approaches establish informative questioning as a learnable behavior, but differ in their information estimators and optimization procedures.
ASIG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hartmann et al., 2026</a>)</cite> amortizes BED into an LLM policy using a generative model derived from the policy’s predictive distributions; its evaluated configuration combines one-step EIG with a multi-step task-outcome reward. We instead explicitly optimize the reasoning preceding design selection and specify the training generative model independently of the policy, using a fixed contrastive prior and a separate semantic likelihood evaluator. This construction enables expected information rewards over the finite hypothesis and outcome spaces, which we accumulate into information-only multi-step returns.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Amortized sequential experimental design.</span>
Policy-based BED learns adaptive designs across an experiment, shifting optimization to training and accounting for the information available from future observations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivanova et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. This includes both tractable-likelihood and implicit-simulator settings. Semi-amortized approaches additionally refine a pretrained design policy using observations from the ongoing experiment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hedman et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We build on the fully amortized formulation, studying how its policy, generative model, and information objective should be instantiated for reasoning LLMs with natural-language actions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task-oriented exploration and interaction learning.</span>
Complementary approaches train curious or collaborative agents using task-oriented rewards, including objectives that assess the consequences of an action through future interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tajwar et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Successful interaction traces also provide supervision for learning clarifying questions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andukuri et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. These works show that strategic information gathering can be learned without an explicit BED objective, and that learned behavior can transfer across tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tajwar et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Our focus is instead on the construction of information-only training returns and their effect on acquisition, reasoning, and transfer.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">External models for information gathering.</span>
Prior work combines language models with parametric Bayesian preference models or learned predictive models for adaptive elicitation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Handa et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Retriever-coupled approaches similarly derive question-training signals from an external candidate distribution or retrieval objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. These provide precedents for separating language generation from information-value estimation. Our construction uses a specified finite hypothesis space and a separate semantic likelihood evaluator during training, while deployment requires neither that hypothesis space nor retrieval-based question selection.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Estimating information value.</span>
Variational and contrastive objectives make Bayesian design optimization tractable <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, while nested Monte Carlo analysis characterizes challenges in estimating information utilities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rainforth et al., 2018</a>)</cite>; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rainforth et al. (2024)</a></cite> survey these approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Extended Experimental Results</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Contrastive set ablations</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A larger contrastive set improves performance.</span>
Figure <a href="#A2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ B.1 Contrastive set ablations ‣ Appendix B Extended Experimental Results ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> compares 100- and 200-animal training generative models. On Animals, their EIG per question is nearly identical (<math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.330" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.330</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.330</annotation></semantics></math> nats), while the 200-animal policy has a slightly higher final solve rate (<math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="43.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>43.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">43.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> versus <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="41.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>41.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">41.3\%</annotation></semantics></math>). The clearest difference is on Plants, where the larger set improves EIG from <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.260" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.260</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.260</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.268" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.268</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.268</annotation></semantics></math> and solve rate from <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="28.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>28.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">28.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>40.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40.7\%</annotation></semantics></math>. It also improves country EIG and solve rate; celebrity EIG is essentially unchanged. These results suggest that increasing the size of the contrastive set can improve the usefulness of the training signal and its transfer, but does not guarantee better acquisition on every domain.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coverage matters beyond the number of hypotheses.</span>
Restricting the training generative model to 100 Mammals substantially reduces performance relative to 100 diverse Animals. On animal evaluation targets, EIG falls from <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.330" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.330</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.330</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.245" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.245</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.245</annotation></semantics></math> and solve rate from <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="41.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>41.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">41.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16.7\%</annotation></semantics></math>; both metrics are also lower on all three OOD domains. Since this condition restricts both the contrastive set and sampled training targets, it tests generative-model coverage rather than a change to the estimator alone. The result reinforces the design choice in Sec. <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 How should the generative model 𝑝(𝜃,𝑦,𝑥) be constructed? ‣ 4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>: decoupling the generative model from the policy allows its coverage to be controlled, but the resulting information reward is only as useful as the distinctions represented during training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.20832v1/result3b_contrastive_coverage.svg" id="A2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/235;" width="548" height="235"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="A2.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training-distribution size and coverage affect acquisition and transfer.</span>
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Expected versus realized information rewards</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span>
We compare one-step reasoning policies trained on the same sampled animal-game states with the same 200-animal contrastive set. The policies differ only in whether the reward marginalizes over hypotheses and possible answers or uses the information gain realized along the sampled trajectory. Both policies generate a reasoning trace before selecting a question; this comparison changes the reward estimator, not which part of the output is optimized.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Expected information rewards usually provide the stronger training signal.</span>
Figure <a href="#A2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ B.2 Expected versus realized information rewards ‣ Appendix B Extended Experimental Results ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> compares information acquisition and solve rate on Animals and three transfer domains. Expected-reward training improves animal EIG from <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.290" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.290</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.290</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.330" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.330</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.330</annotation></semantics></math> nats per question and solve rate from <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="34.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>34.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">34.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="43.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>43.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">43.3\%</annotation></semantics></math>, and improves both metrics on Plants and Countries. The exception is Celebrities, where realized-reward training yields slightly higher EIG and a higher solve rate (<math id="A2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="23.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>23.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">23.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> versus <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="17.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>17.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17.3\%</annotation></semantics></math>). The overall pattern is consistent with the variance-reduction motivation in Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 How should the reward be assigned? ‣ 4 Method: Amortizing BED in Reasoning LLMs ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, but does not establish variance as the sole cause or imply a uniform advantage across transfer domains.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.20832v1/result3c_expected_vs_realized.svg" id="A2.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/235;" width="548" height="235"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="A2.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Expected rewards generally improve learning over realized rewards.</span> One-step reasoning policies trained with the same 200-animal generative model, differing in reward estimator. Expected rewards improve EIG per question and solve rate on Animals, Plants, and Countries, but not Celebrities. Bars and bands show mean <math id="A2.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> SEM over three evaluation repeats.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Non-myopic information acquisition</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate multi-step rewards in three complementary ways: a controlled environment where context must be acquired before it becomes useful, prediction of target attributes during open-ended questioning, and information acquisition in Twenty Questions. The Cube-NM experiment isolates the ability to learn an initially uninformative action; the other evaluations examine whether a longer reward horizon also benefits natural-language policies.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.3.1 </span>Cube-NM: acquiring context before information</h4>

<div id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A controlled non-myopic environment.</span>
We adapt Cube-NM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schütz et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rückstieß et al., 2013</a>)</cite> as a small mechanism check. Its 32 diseases and three equally likely, disease-independent contexts define 96 disease–context pairs. Each context activates eight tests; a separate context test reveals which block is active but provides zero immediate disease information. A useful policy must therefore trade immediate information for better subsequent acquisition. We use a natural-language test-selection interface without reasoning traces to isolate this routing decision from open-ended question generation and medical knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training and evaluation.</span>
The 25 equal-cost tests comprise three context-dependent blocks of eight tests and one context test. The context is independent of the disease, and outcomes are deterministic given both. The textual interface returns positive, negative, or inconclusive outcomes and the diseases invalidated by the observation; the context test instead lists the informative tests. Test identifiers are randomly permuted once, identically across the matched runs, and the outcome matrix and context-test identity are not initially disclosed. The policy selects one identifier without a reasoning trace. We train <span id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen3-0.6B</span> with GRPO/LoRA for 250 updates at learning rate <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>, sampling 16 states and 16 rollouts per state from a rolling on-policy bank covering turns 0–4. Temperature is 2, the entropy coefficient is 0.02, and <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>. Evaluation uses greedy actions over all 96 disease–context pairs and an exact Bayesian MAP decoder. Total EIG is <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log 32</annotation></semantics></math> minus the mean disease-posterior entropy. These are matched single-training-seed results, not estimates of variability across training runs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The two-step reward learns the initially uninformative context test.</span>
Figure <a href="#A2.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ B.3.1 Cube-NM: acquiring context before information ‣ B.3 Non-myopic information acquisition ‣ Appendix B Extended Experimental Results ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows that the two-step policy learns to select the context test with almost unit probability, while the one-step policy favors an immediately informative disease test. This incurs an initial cost: after one test, Bayesian MAP solve rate is <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.1\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=2</annotation></semantics></math> versus <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=1</annotation></semantics></math>. The two-step policy overtakes after three tests (<math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="27.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>27.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">27.1\%</annotation></semantics></math> versus <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="21.9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>21.9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">21.9\%</annotation></semantics></math>) and reaches <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="75.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>75.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">75.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> versus <math id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> after five. Thus the multi-step reward can learn a design for its downstream benefit, even when its immediate disease-information reward is zero. These matched single-seed results support the intended mechanism, not global optimality or an additional claim about reasoning transfer.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.20832v1/result2_cube_nonmyopic.svg" id="A2.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/163;" width="548" height="163"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span><span id="A2.F6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A controlled confirmation of non-myopic learning in Cube-NM.</span> Left: probability of selecting the initially uninformative context test during training. Center: total EIG under greedy acquisition. Right: Bayesian MAP solve rate. The two-step objective learns to acquire context before disease information, improving later acquisition. These are matched single-seed, no-reasoning policies evaluated on all 96 disease–context pairs; the decoder is Bayesian, not an LLM diagnosis.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.3.2 </span>Why Cube-NM requires non-myopic information acquisition</h4>

<div id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Cube-NM provides a controlled setting in which an action can have zero
immediate information gain about the target while increasing the value of a
subsequent experiment. We use this structure to illustrate why a one-step
information-gain objective cannot assign value to such routing actions, while
a two-step objective can.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span>
Let <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta</annotation></semantics></math> denote the latent disease and let <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> denote an auxiliary context
variable. In Cube-NM, the context is independent of the disease,</p>
<table id="A2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta\perp C." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⟂</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta\perp C.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The disease tests are partitioned into context-dependent blocks
<math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathcal{X}_{c}\}_{c\in\mathcal{C}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{X}_{c}\}_{c\in\mathcal{C}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Tests in <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> are informative
about <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta</annotation></semantics></math> when the active context is <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=c</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, there is a context test <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{\mathrm{ctx}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>ctx</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{\mathrm{ctx}}</annotation></semantics></math> whose outcome reveals
the active context,</p>
<table id="A2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y^{\mathrm{ctx}}=C," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>ctx</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y^{\mathrm{ctx}}=C,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">but does not directly reveal the disease.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For a belief state <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>, define the immediate information value of a test <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> as</p>
<table id="A2.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="r(b,x)=I(\Theta;Y_{x}\mid b,x)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(b,x)=I(\Theta;Y_{x}\mid b,x).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The context test has zero myopic information gain.</span>
Because <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y^{\mathrm{ctx}}=C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>ctx</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y^{\mathrm{ctx}}=C</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta\perp C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⟂</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta\perp C</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
<table id="A2.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r(b_{0},x^{\mathrm{ctx}})=I(\Theta;C)=0," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>ctx</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(b_{0},x^{\mathrm{ctx}})=I(\Theta;C)=0,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the initial belief.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">By construction, there exist disease tests with positive immediate information
gain,</p>
<table id="A2.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
