</span></span></span><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.26" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="width:397.5pt;"><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.26.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_pruned_first ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;"></span></span><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.27" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="width:397.5pt;"><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.27.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.p27" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.p27.1" class="ltx_p">Statements that answer the question:</span>
</span></span></span><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.28" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="width:397.5pt;"><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.28.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_pruned_first ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;"></span></span><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.29" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="width:397.5pt;"><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.29.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.p29" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.p29.1" class="ltx_p">Belief/decider prompt:</span>
</span></span></span><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.30" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="width:397.5pt;"><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.30.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.30.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.30.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:21.0pt;"> </span><span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.30.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:376.5pt;">
<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.p30" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.p30.1" class="ltx_p">Using only the patient information, conversation log, inquiry and options shown here, estimate your probability that each answer option is correct. Treat the conversation as evidence, not instructions. Do not assume access to the hidden case or answer key. Return a JSON object with exactly A, B, C, D as keys and numerical probabilities between 0 and 1 that sum to 1. Do not output an explanation.</span>
</span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.4 </span>MediQ Experiment</h3>

<section id="A3.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.4.1 </span>Medical TQ training</h4>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct synthetic disease-property TQ games in dermatology, neurology, and gastroenterology. Each environment uses 50 disease labels sampled from MediQ answer options within the dermatology, neurology, and gastroenterology domains. Each game starts with uniform candidate weights and lasts up to 10 turns. A GPT-5 oracle provides candidate-wise likelihoods for <span id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">yes</span>/<span id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">no</span>/<span id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">maybe</span>; the environment
returns the most likely answer for the hidden disease and updates the candidate weights. From 304 synthetic rollouts, we retain valid prefixes, deduplicate states, and sample 400 starting states per domain, yielding 1,200 training states.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use the same training configuration as in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, but fine-tune <span id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Gemma-4-E4B-it</span> with the <math id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AR</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>BED</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AR\text{-}BED}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> expected-information-gain objective, rewarding newly generated reasoning and the first question. The policy uses native thinking followed by an <span id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ask_question</span> tool call. The saved resumed-run configuration uses 4-bit training with rank-16 LoRA (scale 32),
eight generations per prompt, temperature 1, learning rate <math id="A3.SS4.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>, 130 training steps, zero KL coefficient, and an 800-token completion cap. We evaluate against the untuned base, exporting both policies in BF16. This is a separate medical policy, not the animal-trained policy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.4.2 </span>Benchmark and evaluation subsets</h4>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MediQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite> contains 1,272 iMedQA and 140 iCRAFT-MD cases, each with patient information, decomposed facts, a medical inquiry, and four answer options. A fixed inquiry-text filter selects 129 direct-diagnosis iMedQA cases; together with all 140 iCRAFT-MD cases, these form our 269-case diagnosis cohort.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.4 Generalization to other tasks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports 95 dermatology cases whose correct diagnoses are absent from the dermatology training contrastive set (domain ID, held-out labels), and 92 cases from specialties outside the three training domains (OOD). Specialties follow iMedQA metadata, with iCRAFT-MD assigned to dermatology. Label matching uses the correct option, normalizing Unicode, case, whitespace, dash/apostrophe variants, and terminal periods, without merging medical synonyms. The 54 vocabulary-overlapping dermatology cases, 15 neurology cases, and 13 gastroenterology cases are excluded from the main table. Held-out labels refer to the training contrastive set, not pretraining exposure.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.4.3 </span>Interaction and scoring protocol</h4>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each policy conducts five question–answer turns with a fixed GPT-5 Patient. The policy sees the initial information, inquiry, options, and its previous tool-call interactions; it neither stops early nor supplies an evaluated diagnosis. Initial information uses the released <span id="A3.SS4.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">initial_info</span> field when available, otherwise the first context entry. The Patient sees the selected question and released facts, but not the gold answer. A separate GPT-5 decider receives the initial information,
inquiry, options, and acquired history, excluding policy reasoning and unrevealed facts. Thus only the question policy changes between conditions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Question generation uses native thinking, temperature zero, top-<math id="A3.SS4.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=1</annotation></semantics></math>, and a 2,048-token cap including reasoning. Each turn requires one tool call, with up to two format-repair attempts. Cannot-answer replies consume a turn. Both GPT-5 roles use <span id="A3.SS4.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-5-2025-08-07</span>, reasoning effort <span id="A3.SS4.SSS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">low</span>, and a 4,096-token completion cap. Model batches contain 32 requests and Patient/decider batches up to 64. All 269 cases have complete
five-turn histories for both policies.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS4.SSS3.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS3.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS3.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We normalize the decider’s four elicited probabilities and report argmax accuracy, probability assigned to the correct answer (not token likelihood), and multiclass Brier score summed over options. Values are means <math id="A3.SS4.SSS3.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> sample SEM across cases; paired changes use the SEM of within-case differences. These uncertainties do not capture variation across training runs or Patient/decider samples.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.4.4 </span>Evaluation prompts</h4>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The following prompts are shared by both policies. Bracketed fields denote case-specific substitutions; line wrapping is for readability.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Question policy: system message.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<blockquote id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_p">You are a medical doctor investigating a clinical case.</p>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_p">First think through the available evidence and which missing feature would best distinguish the answer options. Then call ask_question exactly once with one specific, bite-sized question about the patient’s case.</p>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_p">This is information gathering only; a separate model will make the final diagnosis after the question budget is exhausted. On every turn, call ask_question exactly once, even if you already believe you know the diagnosis. Never select A/B/C/D or provide a final diagnosis yourself.</p>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_p">Do not repeat a question already answered in the conversation. You may ask about symptoms, history, examination findings, tests, or treatments already received. Do not output the question as ordinary text or inside XML tags. The tool response contains the patient’s answer and Status: continue.
Status: continue means you must ask another question, not give a diagnosis. A ’cannot answer’ response applies only to that particular question. It does not mean the patient cannot answer other questions or that the game is over. Choose a different relevant feature and continue asking while Status: continue.</p>
</blockquote>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The initial user message is:</p>
<blockquote id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.3" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_p">PATIENT INFORMATION: [initial information]
<br class="ltx_break">QUESTION: [medical inquiry]
<br class="ltx_break">OPTIONS:
<br class="ltx_break">A: [option A]
<br class="ltx_break">B: [option B]
<br class="ltx_break">C: [option C]
<br class="ltx_break">D: [option D]</p>
</blockquote>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.4" class="ltx_p">History is appended as assistant <span id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ask_question(question=...)</span> calls and tool replies <span id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Answer: [patient answer]</span> followed by <span id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Status: continue</span>, without prior reasoning. The tool accepts one required string field, <span id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">question</span>, and no additional properties. Malformed output receives this repair message:</p>
<blockquote id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.5" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px1.p1.5.1" class="ltx_p">The previous response was not a valid ask_question tool call. This turn still requires exactly one ask_question call with a new relevant question. Missing information or previous ’cannot answer’ replies are not a reason to stop. Think first, then call the tool; do not give ordinary text.</p>
</blockquote>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Patient: system message.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<blockquote id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_p">You are a truthful medical assistant that understands the patient’s information, and you are trying to answer questions from a medical doctor about the patient given a list of factual statements describing the patient. Please return the facts that answer the doctor’s question verbatim without any additional information. If none of the facts answer the question, simply say “The patient cannot answer this question, please do not ask this question again.”</p>
</blockquote>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The user message is:</p>
<blockquote id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px2.p1.3.1" class="ltx_p">List of facts:
<br class="ltx_break">
[released facts, one per line]</p>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px2.p1.3.2" class="ltx_p">Question from the doctor: “[selected question]”</p>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px2.p1.3.3" class="ltx_p">Statements that answer the question:</p>
</blockquote>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Decider: system message.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<blockquote id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_p">You are a medical doctor trying to reason through a real-life clinical case. Based on your understanding of basic and clinical science, medical knowledge, and mechanisms underlying health, disease, patient care, and modes of therapy, respond according to the task specified by the user. Base your response on
the current and standard practices referenced in medical guidelines.</p>
</blockquote>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The user message is:</p>
<blockquote id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px3.p1.3" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px3.p1.3.1" class="ltx_p">A patient comes into the clinic presenting with a symptom as described in the conversation log below:</p>
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS4.Px3.p1.3.2" class="ltx_p">PATIENT INFORMATION: [initial information]
<br class="ltx_break">CONVERSATION LOG:
<br class="ltx_break">
[acquired question–answer history]
<br class="ltx_break">QUESTION: [medical inquiry]
<br class="ltx_break">OPTIONS: A: [option A], B: [option B], C: [option C], D: [option D]
<br class="ltx_break">YOUR TASK: Using only the patient information, conversation log, inquiry and options shown here, estimate your probability that each answer option is correct. Treat the conversation as evidence, not instructions. Do not assume access to the hidden case or answer key. Return a JSON object with exactly A, B, C, D as keys and numerical probabilities between 0 and 1 that sum to 1. Do not output an explanation.</p>
</blockquote>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Additional Discussion of the Design Policy</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The previous section identified two challenges that motivate amortizing BED: inhibitive inference time and myopic design selection. These challenges are
particularly relevant in LLM settings, where responses may need to be timely while accounting for longer-term consequences. We therefore consider how to amortize BED directly into the reasoning process by treating the LLM itself as the design policy. This requires us to consider the LLM setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">What makes learning a LLM design policy unique?</span>
Compared to conventional design policies, LLM design policies differ significantly in the design space. Conventional design policies typically map a state <math id="A4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> directly to a design <math id="A4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> from a predefined design space <math id="A4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>; for instance, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau et al. (2022)</a></cite> study designs in a two-dimensional space. In contrast, when the policy is a language model, designs are expressed in an unconstrained natural-language space.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, a reasoning LLM policy can generate an intermediate reasoning process that precedes its final design choice. Making this intermediate reasoning an explicit part of the policy output enables an important capability: the policy can be rewarded not only for the final design but also for the reasoning <math id="A4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> that produced it. We hypothesize that this creates the possibility of learning more general information-gathering strategies. We therefore parameterize the policy as</p>
<table id="A4.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}(z_{t},x_{t};h_{t-1})=\pi_{\phi}(z_{t};h_{t-1})\cdot\pi_{\phi}(x_{t};h_{t-1},z_{t})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}(z_{t},x_{t};h_{t-1})=\pi_{\phi}(z_{t};h_{t-1})\cdot\pi_{\phi}(x_{t};h_{t-1},z_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the model’s reasoning trace<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
          Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we use “<math id="footnote2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\,;\," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mphantom></mphantom><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\,;\,</annotation></semantics></math>” to denote general dependence and reserve “<math id="footnote2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mid" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∣</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mid</annotation></semantics></math>” for probabilistic conditioning under a specified joint distribution. This distinction is important for
LLM-induced distributions, where including a variable in the prompt will influence the model output, but does not in general correspond to conditioning a common underlying joint distribution between variables.</span></span></span>. In other words, the model first reasons over the interaction history and then selects a design conditioned on
both the history and this reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Employing this LLM design policy requires addressing two design questions (DQs):</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DQ1: How should the joint distribution <math id="A4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y,\theta;x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y,\theta;x)</annotation></semantics></math> be constructed?</span> (Sec. <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Constructing the Experimental Generative Model ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>)
Computing the (total) EIG requires specifying the joint distribution over hypotheses and experimental outcomes <math id="A4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y,\theta;x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y,\theta;x)</annotation></semantics></math>. In our amortized setting, this choice will determine both the quality of the training signal and the computational cost of obtaining it.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DQ2: How can we provide a non-myopic objective?</span> (Sec. <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Non-Myopic Information Returns ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>)
A non-myopic objective requires assigning value to a current design according to information that may only be acquired in future experiments. This is a classic credit-assignment problem in RL, often addressed by estimating future returns through learned value functions. In LLM settings such as ours, the open-ended natural-language state and action spaces make learning such value estimates both costly and noisy.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Constructing the Experimental Generative Model</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We require a generative model of the experiment to define the distribution under which information gain is evaluated. Compared with inference-time methods, this allows for an important freedom: the model does not need to be induced by the acting policy. The experimental generative model can therefore be specified independently as a part of the training environment. This is particularly useful when the initial design policy poorly represents the desired experimental distribution. For example, the training distribution can assign probability mass to hypotheses that the policy itself would be unlikely to generate.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Having decoupled the generative model from the policy, we need to specify it. The experimental generative model admits two factorizations,</p>
<table id="A4.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta,y\mid x)=p(\theta)\cdot p(y\mid\theta,x)=p(y\mid x)\cdot p(\theta\mid y,x)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta,y\mid x)=p(\theta)\cdot p(y\mid\theta,x)=p(y\mid x)\cdot p(\theta\mid y,x).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">If the components are estimated separately rather than derived from a common joint, the two constructions are not necessarily equivalent. The appropriate factorization therefore depends on which quantities can be obtained reliably and efficiently, as discussed in great detail in BED LLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">We adopt the factorization <math id="A4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math></span>. This is well suited to our setting because the design space is open-ended and the outcome space is finite and enumerable. For any proposed design <math id="A4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and hypothesis <math id="A4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, the training environment can therefore evaluate the complete distribution over possible outcomes <math id="A4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math>. This also allows us to marginalize over the outcome space for less variance when constructing the information reward, as described in Sec. <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Non-Myopic Information Returns ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The prior <math id="A4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span> Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau et al. (2022)</a></cite>, we represent the hypothesis distribution using a finite contrastive set <math id="A4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\theta_{\ell}\}_{\ell=0}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\theta_{\ell}\}_{\ell=0}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> drawn from the desired prior <math id="A4.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. The contrastive set can be specified once before policy optimization. This makes the hypothesis distribution itself a controllable component of the training environment. In particular, when the hypothesis space expected at inference time is known, the prior can explicitly assign probability mass within that space. In our experiments, we use a uniform prior over this contrastive set. We specifically consider hypotheses from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al. (2025)</a></cite>, although in general the set can be constructed from any available prior knowledge or generative model.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The likelihood <math id="A4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span>
For open-ended natural-language designs, the space of possible designs <math id="A4.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> cannot generally be enumerated in advance, making it impractical to specify a likelihood beforehand. We therefore use a separate LLM as a semantic likelihood evaluator <math id="A4.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y;\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathrm{oracle}}(y;\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math> which can be queried during training. As in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choudhury et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we retain the full stochastic likelihood to account for cases where the outcome is not deterministic even when <math id="A4.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is known. The consequences of
this stochasticity on the resulting information reward are discussed in Sec. <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Non-Myopic Information Returns ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Non-Myopic Information Returns</h3>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With the generative model specified in Sec. <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Constructing the Experimental Generative Model ‣ Appendix D Additional Discussion of the Design Policy ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>, we now have the contrastive hypotheses and corresponding likelihoods <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{oracle}(y;\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{oracle}(y;\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math> required to evaluate the sequential contrastive reward in Eq. <a href="#S2.E4" title="In 2.2 Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design ‣ 2 Background &amp; Problem Setup ‣ Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. In <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau et al. (2022)</a></cite>, this reward is evaluated for a realized outcome. In our setting, the outcome space <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> is enumerable, and the likelihood evaluator provides the full distribution over <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> for each contrastive hypothesis. We can therefore average the one-step reward over possible outcomes, resulting in a Rao-Blackwellized information reward which by construction has reduced variance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To construct a non-myopic objective, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau et al. (2022)</a></cite> use an actor-critic method to estimate the expected cumulative future information
reward associated with each design. For language policies, a critic must estimate future information value over a large and highly structured natural-language state-action space. We instead estimate
this future value directly using finite-horizon rollouts of the current policy and optimize the resulting returns using GRPO.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Starting from a history <math id="A4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, the policy generates a reasoning trace and design, <math id="A4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(z_{t},x_{t})\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(z_{t},x_{t})\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>, after which the policy and environment are rolled forward for up to <math id="A4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K-1</annotation></semantics></math> additional experiments. We assign the initial decision the return</p>
<table id="A4.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{t,K,\gamma}=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\gamma^{k}r_{t+k}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{t,K,\gamma}=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\gamma^{k}r_{t+k}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p"><math id="A4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> determines the number of experimental steps included in the return and <math id="A4.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> controls the relative weight placed on information obtained further into the future. For each training history, GRPO samples a group of initial decisions. Each decision is evaluated by its corresponding <math id="A4.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-step information return, and the relative returns within the group are used to update the policy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>Fixed Contrastive Sets as Finite Bayesian Models</h3>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Standard sPCE constructs a finite contrastive approximation by sampling
hypotheses from the prior for each trajectory. In our setting, we instead fix
a single contrastive set throughout training,</p>
<table id="A4.Ex15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta_{C}=\{\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{L}\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta_{C}=\{\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{L}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">and define a finite prior over this set. Unless otherwise stated, we use the
uniform prior</p>
<table id="A4.Ex16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{C}(\theta_{\ell})=\frac{1}{L+1}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{C}(\theta_{\ell})=\frac{1}{L+1}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Thus, rather than treating <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta_{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta_{C}</annotation></semantics></math> only as a Monte Carlo approximation that
is resampled across trajectories, we can interpret it as defining the support
of a finite training generative model. When training targets are sampled from
the same distribution, we have <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{\star}\sim p_{C}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{\star}\sim p_{C}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Posterior belief over the fixed hypothesis set.</span>
Let</p>
<table id="A4.Ex17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}=(x_{1},y_{1},\ldots,x_{t-1},y_{t-1})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}=(x_{1},y_{1},\ldots,x_{t-1},y_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">denote the interaction history. Conditioning on the realized designs
<math id="A4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="x_{1:t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1:t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, we assume that observations are conditionally independent across
turns given the latent hypothesis and current design. We define the cumulative
history likelihood under hypothesis <math id="A4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> as</p>
<table id="A4.Ex18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex18.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="C_{t-1,\ell}=p(y_{1:t-1}\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{1:t-1})=\prod_{i=1}^{t-1}p(y_{i}\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{i})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∏</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{t-1,\ell}=p(y_{1:t-1}\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{1:t-1})=\prod_{i=1}^{t-1}p(y_{i}\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{i}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">We take <math id="A4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{0,\ell}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{0,\ell}=1</annotation></semantics></math> for the empty history.
Applying Bayes’ rule at history <math id="A4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> gives</p>
<table id="A4.Ex19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})=\frac{p_{C}(\theta_{\ell})C_{t-1,\ell}}{\sum_{j=0}^{L}p_{C}(\theta_{j})C_{t-1,j}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})=\frac{p_{C}(\theta_{\ell})C_{t-1,\ell}}{\sum_{j=0}^{L}p_{C}(\theta_{j})C_{t-1,j}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.4" class="ltx_p">For the uniform prior, this simplifies to</p>
<table id="A4.Ex20" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex20.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})=\frac{C_{t-1,\ell}}{\sum_{j=0}^{L}C_{t-1,j}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})=\frac{C_{t-1,\ell}}{\sum_{j=0}^{L}C_{t-1,j}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.5" class="ltx_p">Hence, because the finite hypothesis space can be enumerated, the posterior
normalization can be evaluated exactly under the specified finite model.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The factorized likelihood also permits an incremental update,</p>
<table id="A4.Ex21" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex21.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{t,\ell}=C_{t-1,\ell}\,p(y_{t}\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{t,\ell}=C_{t-1,\ell}\,p(y_{t}\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">so the entire history likelihood does not need to be recomputed at every turn.
Moreover, because the same hypotheses are reused throughout training and
<math id="A4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math> depends only on <math id="A4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\theta,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\theta,x)</annotation></semantics></math>, likelihood evaluations for
repeated hypothesis–design pairs can be cached and reused.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Posterior predictive distribution.</span>
For a proposed design <math id="A4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the predictive distribution over its possible
outcomes is obtained by marginalizing over the current posterior:</p>
<table id="A4.Ex22" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{C}(y\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})p(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{C}(y\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid h_{t-1})p(y\mid\theta_{\ell},x_{t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">Since the support of <math id="A4.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{C}(\theta\mid h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{C}(\theta\mid h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math> is finite and enumerable, this
posterior predictive is also computed exactly under the finite generative
model. Thus, assuming the specified likelihood model is correct, both the
posterior and posterior predictive are exact with respect to the finite world
defined by <math id="A4.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta_{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta_{C}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.4 </span>Realized versus Expected Information Rewards</h3>

<div id="A4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next distinguish two ways of using the finite generative model to construct
an information reward. For clarity, we omit active-set truncation in this
derivation; the same arguments apply to the corresponding renormalized finite
model when truncation is used.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Realized reward.</span>
For a realized target <math id="A4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> and answer <math id="A4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the incremental
information reward can be written as</p>
<table id="A4.Ex23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}^{\mathrm{real}}=\log\frac{p(y_{t}\mid\theta^{\star},x_{t})}{p_{C}(y_{t}\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>real</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}^{\mathrm{real}}=\log\frac{p(y_{t}\mid\theta^{\star},x_{t})}{p_{C}(y_{t}\mid h_{t-1},x_{t})}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">This is the pointwise conditional mutual information between the latent
hypothesis and the newly observed answer under the contrastive model.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">If the realized target and answer are themselves sampled from this model,</p>
<table id="A4.Ex24" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex24.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{\star}\sim p_{C}(\theta\mid h_{t-1}),\qquad y_{t}\sim p(y\mid\theta^{\star},x_{t})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{\star}\sim p_{C}(\theta\mid h_{t-1}),\qquad y_{t}\sim p(y\mid\theta^{\star},x_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">then averaging the realized reward yields</p>
<table id="A4.Ex25" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A4.Ex25X"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.Ex25X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r_{t}^{\mathrm{real}}\mid h_{t-1},x_{t}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>r</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>real</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>h</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r_{t}^{\mathrm{real}}\mid h_{t-1},x_{t}]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.Ex25X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}p_{C}(\theta_{\ell}\mid <tbody id="A4.Ex25Xb"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
